title: Adie's Tonic Pupil: A Clinical Deep-Dive
summary: Adie's Tonic Pupil is a common neurological condition involving postganglionic parasympathetic denervation of the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle. This poster provides a textbook-level review of its pathophysiology, pharmacological testing, and critical differentials for the ophthalmic resident.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Adie’s Tonic Pupil is a benign but clinically significant condition caused by damage to the postganglionic parasympathetic fibers in the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves. It is characterized by a mid-dilated pupil that reacts poorly to light but shows a robust, albeit 'tonic' (slow), response to near effort. Most cases are idiopathic, but the underlying pathology involves denervation followed by aberrant regeneration of the nerves originally destined for the ciliary body into the iris sphincter muscle.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: Aberrant Regeneration
content: Step 1: Insult to the Ciliary Ganglion results in parasympathetic denervation of the iris sphincter and ciliary body.
Step 2: Acute phase presents with a large, fixed pupil and loss of accommodation (blurred near vision).
Step 3: Regeneration begins. Normally, fibers to the ciliary body outnumber iris fibers 30:1.
Step 4: Aberrant Rewiring: Fibers originally destined for the ciliary body (near reflex) regrow into the iris sphincter.
Step 5: Result: Light-Near Dissociation. The pupil doesn't react to light but constricts during near effort because the 'near' signal is now sent to the iris.

sections.title: Hallmark Ocular Exam Findings
content: Anisocoria: Greater in bright light than in dim light.
Segmental Iris Palsy: 'Worm-like' (vermiform) movements of the iris border under slit-lamp.
Light-Near Dissociation: Minimal reaction to light, slow tonic constriction to near.
Tonic Redilatation: Pupil takes a long time to return to baseline size after near task.
Tonic Accommodation: Slowness in changing focus from near to far.
Decreased Corneal Sensitivity: If short ciliary nerves are involved.

sections.title: The Pharmacological Gold Standard
content: Step 1: Measure pupil sizes in controlled dim and bright light.
Step 2: Instill Pilocarpine 0.1% or 0.125% (low concentration) in both eyes.
Step 3: Wait 30–45 minutes in a dimly lit room.
Step 4: Positive Result: The Adie pupil constricts significantly; the normal pupil does NOT (due to denervation supersensitivity).
Step 5: Interpretation: Confirms post-ganglionic denervation.

sections.title: RED FLAG: Excluding 3rd Nerve Palsy
content: Sudden onset of 'Down and Out' eye position.
Presence of Ptosis (drooping eyelid).
Acute headache or 'worst headache of life' (Aneurysm risk!).
Total lack of response to BOTH light and near stimuli.
Failure of the pupil to constrict with 0.1% Pilocarpine but constricts with 1% Pilocarpine.

branches: Holmes-Adie: Adie's + Absent Deep Tendon Reflexes (Achilles/Patellar)
Ross Syndrome: Adie's + Hyporeflexia + Segmental Anhidrosis (excessive sweating elsewhere)
Harlequin Syndrome: Unilateral facial flushing and sweating

content.explanation: S - Sectoral palsy (vermiform movements). S - Second decade (most common in young adults). S - Supersensitivity (constricts to dilute 0.125% pilo).

sections.title: Management & Patient Education
content: Reassurance: Condition is benign and usually stabilizes.
Reading Glasses: Unequal accommodation may require a 'plus' lens for the affected eye.
Tinted Lenses: To manage photophobia from the fixed mydriasis.
Weak Pilocarpine (0.1%): May be used for cosmesis or to improve focus, though rarely needed.
Safety: Advise patients that pupillary inequality may be permanent (anisocoria evolves over years).

sections.title: Natural History & Prognosis
sections.content: Initially, the Adie pupil is larger than the fellow eye. Over many years, the pupil undergoes 'Little Old Adie' syndrome—it gradually becomes smaller and may eventually be smaller than the normal pupil in dim light, though it remains non-reactive to light. Bilateral involvement occurs in roughly 4% of patients per year.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The 'Tonic' nature refers to the slow, sustained contraction and even slower redilatation.
If the pupil does NOT constrict with 1% Pilocarpine, it is a 'Pharmacological Pupil' (e.g., Atropine or Scopolamine patch).
Segmental palsy is best seen by turning the slit-lamp beam 90 degrees and observing the iris margin.
Always check Deep Tendon Reflexes (DTRs) in the clinic for any new tonic pupil diagnosis.
Adie's is a diagnosis of exclusion; ensure no history of trauma or use of sympathomimetics.
